most of their battles here, in the yard or two between "released" and "broken," and that's
why coaches say a route is won before the break, not at it.

### The break and the catch point

The **break** is the cut itself, and its quality decides how much separation the receiver
has when the ball arrives. A sharp break (sink the hips, plant, explode the other way)
creates space against a defender who is mirroring. A rounded break keeps speed, as in the
speed out, and works against a defender who is backing up. Either way, on a quick throw the
ball is usually already in the air.

Then comes the **catch point**: the moment the ball and the receiver's hands meet. If the
release, stem and break were good, it's an easy catch with the defender a step or two away.
If not, it's a
[**contested catch**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-contested-catch): a catch made with a
defender close enough to touch the ball or the receiver's hands. FTN's charters flagged about
14% of 2025 targets as contested; only about 42% of those were caught, against about 71% of
the rest.[^contested] The quick game is designed to avoid contested catches: a well-run
slant-flat or stick throws to the receiver who is *not* covered. When a quick throw becomes a
contested catch, usually against press-man coverage with no open receiver, the offense is
relying on a receiver who can win at the catch point, and on a quarterback willing to throw
him the ball anyway. Throws placed where only the receiver can reach them, like the
[back-shoulder throw](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd),
are how good pairs make those catches more likely.

### The double move: punishing the defender who guesses right

The quick game creates its own counter. A cornerback who has watched film of an offense
throwing slant after slant and hitch after hitch learns to sit on those routes, and to jump
them the instant the receiver breaks. That is exactly the defender a
[**double move**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-move) is built for. The
receiver fakes a quick route, the quarterback often pump-fakes (starts his throwing motion
without letting go) as if throwing it, and when the defender drives on the fake, the receiver
turns up the field behind him. The common forms are named for their two parts: slant-and-go (the
[sluggo](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)), out-and-up, hitch-and-go, the stutter-go (a fake
stop), and the stick-nod, in which the stick runner fakes settling and then breaks up the field,
the counter to a flat defender who has learned to drive on the stick.

The double move is the quick game's insurance policy: without it, a defense could squeeze the
short routes harder every week; with it, every corner who jumps a slant risks a long touchdown.
The cost is time. A double move takes three seconds or more, so offenses tend to call it with an
extra blocker, after they have thrown the short version often enough to bait the defender.

## Quick screens: now and bubble

The quick game has two close cousins that aren't really passes in the usual sense. Both are
screens, throws to a receiver behind or at the line of scrimmage with teammates blocking in
front of him, and both are thrown the instant the ball is snapped. (Slower screens to running
backs and tight ends, with linemen releasing to block, are in
[Play-Action, Bootlegs, and Screens](04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd).)

A [**now screen**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-now-screen) goes to an outside receiver.
He takes a step back (or none) and catches the ball a second after the snap, while the
receiver inside him blocks the nearest defender. Teams call versions of it a
[smoke screen](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-smoke-screen) or a
[quick screen](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-quick-screen); the names vary by playbook
(some use "smoke" for the version with no blocker at all), but the idea is the same.

```{python}
#| label: fig-now
#| fig-cap: "A now screen against off coverage, the offense's left side. The cornerback lines up eight yards off X, so X catches the ball about a second after the snap and is already running before the cornerback can close. H blocks the slot defender ($), the only other defender nearby. The box holds six defenders, so outside it on this side the defense has just the cornerback and the $ underneath, with a safety twelve yards deep. The quarterback can decide this before the snap from the cushion alone."
off = spread()
dfn = cover3(nb_side=-1, cb_d=8.0, cb_out=0.5,
             extra={"NB": (5.0, -7.8), "SS": (12.0, 9.0), "FS": (12.0, -9.0)})
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.route("X", [(0, 0), (-1.0, 0.3)], speed=3.0)
p.run("X", [(5.5, 1.2)], delay=0.15)
go_to(p, "H", (3.3, -8.6), kind="block")
p.pass_to("X", t=0.35)
p.drop("LCB", (6.5, -15.2), delay=0.25)
p.highlight("LCB")
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-25.0, 7.5), window=(-8.5, 15.5))
vbracket(fld, p, -17.8, -0.7, 8.0)
say(fld, p, 3.6, -21.4, "8-yard\ncushion:\nfree yards", fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 0.9, -11.2, "H blocks\nthe $", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -3.6, -11.0, "ball out at once:\nno drop, no read", color=style.BALL, fontsize=7)
bracket(fld, p, 6.8, -5.6, 5.6, "6 in the box", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, dy=1.1)
legend(fld.fig, ["route", "block", "run", "pass"], y=0.07)
plt.show()
```

The now screen exists to punish one thing: **a defender playing far off the ball.** An
eight-yard cushion is eight yards the defender has to cover before he can make a tackle, and
a receiver who catches the ball at the snap gets to spend those yards running instead. Many
offenses attach the now screen to ordinary plays as an extra option (coaches say they *tag* it
on), so that the quarterback, seeing the cornerback backed up eight yards, can throw it as a free
five yards instead of running the called play. The ball comes out at once for a rules reason too:
the receivers who block for it may not block a defender more than a yard past the line before the
pass is thrown, the same one-yard limit that governs rubs.

The [**bubble screen**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bubble-screen) is the inside
version. A slot receiver drifts a step or two back and then out toward the sideline, a path
that looks like a bubble when you draw it, and catches the ball already running, while the
receivers outside him turn and block.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bubble
#| fig-cap: "A bubble screen to the trips side, on the offense's right. H, the middle of three receivers (#2), bows back and out and catches the ball on the run, already moving toward the sideline. Z (#1) blocks the cornerback and Y, the tight end on the inside (#3), blocks the slot defender ($). Outside the box on that side the offense has three players (two blockers and the ball carrier) against two defenders; the third, the safety (SS), starts twelve yards deep. Before the snap, the quarterback counted those numbers."
def trips_right():
    """11 personnel, gun trips right: Y (the tight end, #3) and H (#2) off the ball, Z (#1) on the line."""
    return line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, -1.5, "R"), O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0),
                      O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 8.5), O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 13.0), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 19.0)]


dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"),
       D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.0, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.2, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 2.6, "M"),
       D("NB", "NB", 5.5, 12.0, "$"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 21.2, "CB"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"),
       D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 12.0, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -8.0, "FS")]
p = Play(trips_right(), dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
protect(p)
p.route("H", [(0, 0), (-1.6, 2.0), (-1.8, 4.0)], speed=6.0)
p.run("H", [(1.5, 1.2), (5.8, 1.6), (10.8, 1.8)])
go_to(p, "Z", (5.0, 20.8), kind="block")
go_to(p, "Y", (4.2, 11.4), kind="block")
p.pass_to("H", t=0.45)
p.highlight("H")
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-10.5, 26.0), window=(-8.5, 19.5))
bracket(fld, p, 15.6, 7.0, 22.5, "outside the box: 3 offensive players vs 2 defenders\n(the safety starts 12 yards deep)",
        fontsize=7, dy=1.3)
say(fld, p, -5.6, 12.0, "bubble: a step\nback, then out", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
legend(fld.fig, ["route", "block", "run", "pass"], y=0.07)
plt.show()
```

Coaches who throw these screens on almost every snap, as many college offenses do and some
NFL offenses do, often teach the decision with three words: **numbers, leverage, grass.**

- **Numbers:** count the defenders outside the box on one side and compare them with the
  offense's players there. Three against two is a screen. This is the
  [box count](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd) seen from
  the other side: every defender a defense puts in the box to stop the run is one fewer
  outside it.
- **Leverage:** can the blockers get between their defenders and the ball carrier? A
  defender lined up inside, near the ball, is easy to block from the outside; one lined up
  wide is not.
- **Grass:** how much space is there between the ball carrier and the nearest unblocked
  defender? A safety twelve yards deep is twelve yards of grass.

That is why quick screens are often thought of as part of the run game, and why they are so
often packaged with runs. If the defense puts a seventh or eighth man in the box to stop the
run, someone outside the box has left, and the screen to that side gets better. When the
quarterback decides between the run and the screen *after* the snap, by reading a defender, the
play becomes a [run-pass option](04-06-rpos.qmd), and the bubble attached to a run is one of the
most common RPOs in football ([bubble RPO](04-06-rpos.qmd)).

One rule detail makes the bubble unusual. Because it is often thrown sideways or slightly
backward, a bubble that is thrown behind the receiver is a backward pass, and a backward
pass that hits the ground is a live ball, not an incompletion: either team can recover it.[^backward]
That's why you sometimes see a defender scoop up a dropped bubble and run the other way, and
why offenses want the throw to be clearly forward or clearly caught.

## The answer to press and blitz

Now put the chapter together. The two most aggressive things a defense can do against the
pass are to **blitz** (send more rushers than the offense can comfortably block) and to
**press** (jam receivers to destroy the timing). Both are bets that the quarterback won't get
the ball out in time. The quick game is the offense taking that bet.

The arithmetic of a blitz explains why. A [five-man pressure](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd)
sends five rushers. Keep six men in to block (the five linemen and the back) and the offense can
pick up all five with a man to spare. Keep only five and it can still block five rushers on paper,
but only if the protection is aimed at the right five. Protections are set before the snap by
counting the defenders who *might* rush ([Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd)'s
[slide](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slide-protection) and Mike identification). If the line
slides toward two linebackers and one of them drops into coverage while a defender from the other
edge comes, one blocker is left with nobody and one rusher has no blocker at all: a
[free rusher](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-free-rusher). Send six against five and somebody is
free no matter what. Either way the protection's rule is that the free man belongs to the
quarterback. He is "hot": the ball has to come out before he arrives, on a
[hot route](04-02-pass-protection.qmd) or a [sight adjustment](04-02-pass-protection.qmd) aimed at
the area the blitzer just left.

Behind the blitz, the coverage is thin. It is often man coverage, pressed, with one safety deep
or none, or a [fire zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fire-zone) (three deep defenders and
three underneath, built in [Zone Blitz and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)).
In either case the blitzer's old spot is empty. A quick throw attacks every part of that: it beats
the free rusher to the quarterback, and it goes to a receiver who is alone in coverage or running
into the hole the blitzer left.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pressure
#| fig-cap: "Quick game against a five-man pressure (simulated tracking in the Big Data Bowl format). The defense shows press-man coverage with one deep safety (Cover 1), with the Mike linebacker (M) walked up over the center as a possible sixth rusher. The running back releases into a route, so the offense has five blockers, and the line slides right toward the Mike: the left tackle takes the end in front of him, the left guard the tackle, and the center, right guard and right tackle step right. At the snap the Mike drops out to cover the back, so the center has nobody, and the slot defender ($, ringed in orange) blitzes off the offense's left edge, where nobody is left to block him. He is the quarterback's man: hot. X (ringed in green) beats the press cornerback with an inside release, which costs him a beat, and breaks in on a slant into the area the blitzer left. The ball is out 2.1 seconds after the snap, a beat before the blitzer gets there."
def pressure_play():
    off = spread(rb_w=1.5)
    dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"),
           D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -4.0, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 2.2, 0.6, "M"),
           D("NB", "NB", 4.5, -10.5, "$"), D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.6, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 15.6, "CB"),
           D("SS", "SS", 6.0, 8.6, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
    # a five-man slide right: LT and LG take the two linemen in front of them, C/RG/RT step to their right
    for k, (dd, ww) in (("LT", (-1.3, -1.4)), ("LG", (-1.0, 0.2)), ("C", (-1.0, 1.3)), ("RG", (-1.0, 1.0)),
                        ("RT", (-1.2, 1.2))):
        p.block(k, pts=[(dd, ww)], speed=4.0)
        p.block(k, pts=[(-0.4, 0.0)], speed=0.6)
    for k in ("WDE", "WDT", "SDT", "SDE"):           # the four linemen rush and engage them
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=4.0)
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-0.4, 0.0)], speed=0.6)
    p.dropback(2.0, speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "NB", (-6.4, -1.4), kind="rush", speed=6.3, delay=0.2, via=[(1.0, -7.2)])
    p.route("RB", r.path((0.5, 4.5), (1.4, 8.5), (5.0, 10.5), (6.0, 11.5)), side=1)
    p.man("MIKE", "RB")
    # X: a jab outside against the press corner, an inside release through his hands, then the stem and slant
    p.route("X", [(0, 0), (0.2, 0.8)], speed=2.4)
    p.route("X", [(0, 0), (2.2, -1.6)], speed=4.4)                 # hand-fight through the jam
    p.route("X", [(0, 0), (3.4, -0.2)], speed=4.4)                 # re-accelerate up the stem
    p.route("X", [(0, 0), (4.2, -5.8), (5.4, -8.0)], speed=6.6)    # the break and the slant
    p.route("H", r.seam(18.0))
    p.man("WILL", "H")
    p.route("Y", r.hitch(6.0))
    p.man("SS", "Y")
    p.route("Z", r.go(16.0))
    p.man("RCB", "Z")
    p.drop("FS", (14.0, 0.0))
    p.pass_to("X", t=2.1)
    trail(p, "LCB", "X", jab=(1.3, -16.2), off=(-0.9, -0.9), t_on=1.1)  # bites on the jab, then chases from behind
    return p


pz = pressure_play()
t_c = catch_time(pz)
_tr = tracking(pz)
_f = _tr[np.isclose(_tr["time"], 2.1)]
gap = float(np.hypot(*(_f.loc[_f.displayName == "NB", ["x", "y"]].values[0]
                       - _f.loc[_f.displayName == "QB", ["x", "y"]].values[0])))
notes = ["The line slides right, toward the M.\nThe $ starts in the slot.",
         "M drops to cover the back, so C has\nnobody. The $ is free: he's hot.",
         f"Ball out at 2.1 s as X comes out of\nhis break; the $ is still {gap:.0f} yd away.",
         "Caught in front of the trailing CB,\nin the space the $ left."]
play_movie(pz, [0.0, 1.0, 2.1, t_c], notes=notes, lateral=(-24.0, 8.0), window=(-9.0, 13.5),
           rings=(("NB", style.DEFENSE_DARK), ("X", style.THIRD)), throw_t=2.1)
```

Three details in that play are worth slowing down for. First, the quarterback knew before the
snap where the ball was likely to go. Pressed corners with a single safety deep is a classic
pressure look, and the slot defender creeping toward the line told him which area might empty.
His pre-snap plan was "if the $ comes, the ball goes to X, inside, right now." Second, he
confirmed it with one look after the snap. The $ might have been bluffing, showing a blitz and
then backing out into coverage; the moment he crossed the line of scrimmage, the plan was on.
Had he backed out, the quarterback would simply have run the play's normal read. Third, the
slant was the right route for the press cornerback's leverage: he lined up on X's outside, so an
inside release was the release X could win. That release cost X a beat (against off coverage
the same slant would come out around 1.2 to 1.5 seconds), which is why this ball left at 2.1:
still on time for X, still ahead of the blitz.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rush-epa
#| fig-cap: "What the quick game is worth against the blitz. Every 2025 regular-season dropback with a charted number of pass rushers, sorted by the rush (four or fewer, or five or more) and by the outcome: a pass out in under 2.5 seconds (blue), or anything slower, sacks and scrambles included (grey). The bars are expected points added (EPA) per dropback; the thin lines are 95% confidence intervals. Against five or more rushers, quick throws gained about a third of a point more per dropback than everything else. A caution on reading it: quarterbacks hold the ball longer partly *because* nobody is open, so this comparison flatters quick throws; it shows the size of the stakes, not a controlled experiment."
d = DB25[DB25["number_of_pass_rushers"].notna() & DB25["epa"].notna()].copy()
quick = (d["pass_attempt"] == 1) & (d["sack"] == 0) & (d["time_to_throw"] < 2.5)
held = (d["sack"] == 1) | (d["qb_scramble"] == 1) | ((d["pass_attempt"] == 1) & (d["time_to_throw"] >= 2.5))
d["outcome"] = np.select([quick, held], ["quick", "held"], default="unknown")
d = d[d["outcome"] != "unknown"]
d["rush"] = np.where(d["number_of_pass_rushers"] >= 5, "Five or more rushers", "Four or fewer rushers")
g = d.groupby(["rush", "outcome"])["epa"].agg(["mean", "std", "size"])
g["se"] = g["std"] / np.sqrt(g["size"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 2.9))
rows = ["Four or fewer rushers", "Five or more rushers"]
for i, rush in enumerate(rows):
    for j, (oc, col, lab) in enumerate((("quick", style.OFFENSE, "ball out in under 2.5 s"),
                                         ("held", style.MUTED, "held 2.5 s or longer, or sacked / scrambled"))):
        m, se, n = g.loc[(rush, oc), ["mean", "se", "size"]]
        y = i + (0.19 if j == 0 else -0.19)
        ax.barh(y, m, height=0.34, color=col, label=lab if i == 0 else None, zorder=2)
        ax.errorbar(m, y, xerr=1.96 * se, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, capsize=2, zorder=3)
        x_txt = max(m, 0) + 1.96 * se + 0.012
        ax.text(x_txt, y, f"{m:+.2f}  (n = {int(n):,})", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK)
ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
ax.set_yticks([0, 1], rows, fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlim(-0.2, 0.42)
ax.set_xlabel("Expected points added per dropback", fontsize=8.5)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.42, -0.25), fontsize=7.6, ncol=2)
ax.set_title("Against the blitz, the ball that comes out fast is worth the most (2025)", fontsize=9.5, loc="left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The chart puts a number on the trade.[^rushepa] Against a standard four-man rush, a quick
throw was worth about an eighth of a point more than a slower outcome. Against five or more
rushers, the gap roughly doubles: quick throws gained about +0.23 expected points per
dropback, while everything slower, with the sacks that a blitz produces, averaged about
-0.10. A blitz is a coin flip the defense is offering, and a quarterback who gets the ball out
before the extra rusher arrives wins the flip far more often than he loses it.

So why do defenses blitz at all, on about one dropback in four? Because pooled over every
outcome, the bet is roughly even. In 2025, dropbacks against five or more rushers averaged about
+0.05 expected points for the offense, against +0.04 for four or fewer: a hair worse for the
defense, within the noise, but with more sacks (about 7.8% of dropbacks against 6.0%). And
blitzes come more often on third down (about 30% of dropbacks, against 25% on first and second),
where forcing a short throw that falls short of the line to gain is a win in itself. The blitz is a variance play: it produces sacks
and hurried incompletions, and it gives up the quick completion into the space it vacated. That is
why blitz-happy defenses spend so much effort disguising when and where the pressure will come
from ([Blitz and Man Pressure](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd) does the math
from the defense's side; [Zone Blitz and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)
the disguises).

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game, the blitz is a button you press to make the other player panic. In the NFL,
a quarterback who sees six defenders at the line is usually not panicking; his offense has
spent the week on what to do when that happens. Every quick concept is installed with its blitz
answer: which receiver becomes hot (the ball goes to him at once, often on a shortened version
of his route) if a particular defender comes, which routes become sight adjustments, and which
rusher, if any, the protection call leaves unblocked. The real contest is whether the defense
can *hide* the blitz until it's too late to adjust, or show one and not bring it. That's why
the pre-snap dance of defenders walking up and backing out, covered in
[The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd), matters so much.
:::

## Film room: three offenses that lived on it

The quick game is in every playbook, but a few offenses built their identity on it. Each of
the three below shows a different reason to.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: New Orleans Saints 2017–2019"}
**The quick game as accuracy.** Late in Drew Brees's career, the engine of Sean Payton's offense
(Payton was head coach 2006–2021, Brees the quarterback 2006–2020) was the short, on-time throw.
Brees broke the NFL's single-season completion-percentage record in 2017 (72.0%) and broke it
again in 2018 (74.4%).[^brees] In 2019, among quarterbacks with 300 or more attempts, he had the
second-fastest average time to throw and one of the shortest average throws (about 6.5 yards),
and Michael Thomas set the single-season receptions record with 149, about seven in ten of them on
throws that traveled less than ten yards in the air.[^thomas]

**What to notice on the tape:** the ball leaving on Brees's last step, again and again, and
Thomas getting inside the cornerback on the slant, then shielding the ball with his body at the
catch point.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: New England Patriots 2007–2012"}
**The quick game as an option tree.** The Tom Brady–era Patriots ran it through a small, quick
slot receiver. Wes Welker caught 112 passes in 2007, 123 in 2009 and 122 in 2011, leading the
league three times in five years,[^welker] most of them within a few yards of the line, many on
option routes in which he read his defender's leverage and broke away from it, the same rule the
stick route uses. Brady's clock stayed fast long after: in 2022, at 45, he had the fastest
average time to throw of any regular starter.[^brady]

**What to notice on the tape:** Welker inside, a defender over him trying to guess his break,
and Brady throwing as Welker turned his head, before the break had finished.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Kansas City Chiefs 2022–2024"}
**The quick game as an adaptation.** In 2018, Patrick Mahomes's first season as the starter, the
Chiefs threw deep more than almost anyone, with Tyreek Hill as the threat. Defenses adjusted
first. Their throws were already getting shorter in 2019, 2020 and 2021, with Hill still on the
roster, as opponents played two deep safeties to take away the big play: by 2021, Kansas City saw
a two-high shell on about 46% of its dropbacks, third-most in the league.[^kc2high] Then Hill was
traded to Miami in March 2022,[^hill] and over the next three seasons Andy Reid rebuilt the
offense around shorter throws to Travis Kelce and a rotating cast of receivers. By 2023 and 2024
the Chiefs' average throw was the second-shortest in the league (the chart after this box shows
the whole slide). They won the Super Bowl after the
2022 and 2023 seasons anyway.


**What to notice on the tape:** Kelce, lined up in the slot or as the innermost receiver of
trips, running a stick or an option route at five to eight yards and settling between two zone
defenders, with Mahomes throwing as he turns. Nearly three of every four of Kelce's targets in
2022 traveled less than ten yards in the air.[^kc] For one clip, find Super Bowl LVII (February
12, 2023, against Philadelphia): in the fourth quarter, on third-and-goal from the 4, Skyy Moore
went in motion, reversed and ran to the flat, and Mahomes threw it to him for a touchdown
1.7 seconds after the snap, against a defense charted as Cover 0 with seven rushers. The
Chiefs had scored on the same motion play, run to the other side to Kadarius Toney, less than three
minutes of game clock earlier.[^sb57] That's the quick game at its purest: everybody coming, nobody deep, and the ball
gone before it matters.

The 2025 point on the chart below matters too: with a different set of receivers, the Chiefs' depth
went back to about the league median. The quick game here was never a fixed identity; it was a
great offense taking what the defenses of those years left underneath.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-kc-adot
#| fig-cap: "The Chiefs' average depth of target (how far past the line of scrimmage the ball was thrown, on average) by season, 2016–2025, against the league: the grey band holds the middle 80% of teams and the grey line is the median team. Kansas City went from one of the deepest-throwing teams in 2018 (fifth of 32) to second-shallowest in 2023 and 2024. The slide began in 2019, with Tyreek Hill still on the roster, and deepened after his trade in March 2022 (shaded seasons), with Travis Kelce at the center of the short game; in 2025 the Chiefs were back at about the median. Regular season, sacks and spikes excluded; nflverse play-by-play."
cols = ["season", "season_type", "posteam", "pass_attempt", "sack", "qb_spike", "air_yards"]
pl = pbp(list(range(2016, 2026)), columns=cols)
att = pl[(pl["season_type"] == "REG") & (pl["pass_attempt"] == 1) & (pl["sack"] == 0) & (pl["qb_spike"] != 1)
         & pl["air_yards"].notna()]
team = att.groupby(["season", "posteam"])["air_yards"].mean().unstack()
kc, med = team["KC"], team.median(axis=1)
rank = team.rank(axis=1, ascending=False)["KC"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.2))
ax.axvspan(2021.5, 2024.5, color=style.OFFENSE_TINT, alpha=0.55, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.fill_between(team.index, team.quantile(0.1, axis=1), team.quantile(0.9, axis=1), color=style.GRID, alpha=0.9,
                lw=0, label="middle 80% of teams", zorder=1)
ax.plot(med.index, med.values, color=style.MUTED, lw=1.6, label="median team", zorder=2)
ax.plot(kc.index, kc.values, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=5, label="Kansas City", zorder=3)
for yr, dy in ((2018, 10), (2021, -22), (2023, -22), (2024, -22)):
    ax.annotate(f"{kc[yr]:.1f} yd\n(rank {int(rank[yr])})", (yr, kc[yr]), xytext=(0, dy), textcoords="offset points",
                ha="center", fontsize=7.3, color=style.INK, linespacing=1.1)
ax.text(2023, 9.95, "after the Hill trade", ha="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
ax.set_xticks(range(2016, 2026))
ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Average depth of target (yd)", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_ylim(5.0, 10.4)
ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.1), fontsize=7.5, ncol=3)
ax.set_title("The Chiefs' throws got shorter (rank 1 = deepest of 32)", fontsize=9.5, loc="left")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: one-two-throw"}
**Before the snap**

- **The corners.** Off or pressed? Inside or outside the receiver? A corner seven yards off
  with outside leverage is inviting a slant or a now screen; a pressed corner is daring the
  receiver to beat him off the line.
- **The slot defender.** Where is the man between the slot receiver and the box? He is the
  read on almost every quick concept to that side. If he walks up toward the line, think
  blitz, and think quick throw.
- **Count outside the box.** Three receivers against two defenders on one side, with the
  safety far away, is a screen waiting to happen.

**At the snap: the stopwatch.** Count "one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two" from the snap. If the
ball is gone before you finish "two," you just watched the quick game working as designed. Count a
dozen dropbacks in a game and you'll find that roughly half of them are out before
"two-and-a-half."

**At the snap: watch the linemen.** Three plays come out in about a second, and the linemen tell
them apart. On a quick throw they set to pass-block, short and aggressive, and stay at the line.
On a run-pass option they fire forward as if blocking a run. On a now or bubble screen the
*receivers* near the ball turn and block.

**After the throw**

- On the replay, find the one defender between the two receivers on the side the ball went.
  Did he widen, sink or sit? The ball went to the receiver he didn't take.
- When the defense blitzes, watch where the ball goes. Usually it goes quickly to the area the
  blitzer came from.

**For your prediction log** ([How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)):
before each third-and-short-to-medium, write *quick* or *not quick*, and the side you expect,
based on the corners' leverage. Then time the throw.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: pick a side"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-side
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-6. The offense has called slant-flat to both sides (outside receiver on a slant, slot receiver to the flat) and left the choice of side to the quarterback."
off = spread()
dfn = cover3(nb_side=-1, extra={"RCB": (1.3, 14.2), "SS": (3.5, 12.0), "NB": (5.0, -7.0)})
p = Play(off, dfn, los=45, to_go=6)
protect(p)
p.dropback(1.5)
for k in ("X", "Z"):
    p.route(k, r.slant(stem=3.0, length=9.0))
for k in ("H", "Y"):
    p.route(k, r.path((1.0, 1.8), (3.0, 10.0)))
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-25.0, 25.0), window=(-8.5, 15.5))
plt.show()
```

**Which side should the quarterback pick, and which defender does he watch after the snap?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The left side, reading the slot defender ($).** Run through the pre-snap read on each side.

On the **right**, both routes are in trouble before the snap. The cornerback is pressed with
inside leverage, sitting right where Z's slant wants to go, so Z has to beat a jam *and* get
across the cornerback's face; and the safety has already widened to the flat, standing where
Y's flat route ends. One defender is in each receiver's path.

On the **left**, the cornerback is seven yards off and outside X, which concedes the slant
(away from leverage), and the slot defender is inside H, the one man who has to choose between
the two routes. That's the slant-flat picture from earlier in the chapter. After the snap the
quarterback watches only the $: if he widens with H, throw the slant; if he sits, throw the flat.

Doesn't the right side have its own answer? A corner pressing with inside leverage invites an
outside release and the fade, and Z might win it. But the fade isn't in this call, and even when
it is, it's a lower-percentage throw against a corner who is right on top of the receiver. On the
left, the play works exactly as designed, with two receivers against one defender and an easy
read. The quarterback takes the side where the concept he called is already winning.

This is why offenses call a quick concept to both sides. The defense has to give something
away somewhere, and the quarterback's pre-snap job is to find where.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: six at the line"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-zero
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-5, just before the snap. The offense has five linemen, and a running back who can stay in to block or go out for a pass."
off = spread()
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -5.4, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"),
       D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.4, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.9, -2.3, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 1.9, 0.8, "M"),
       D("NB", "NB", 3.0, -8.6, "$"), D("SS", "SS", 3.0, 8.6, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 6.0, 0.6, "FS"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 1.3, -13.8, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.3, 13.8, "CB")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=50, to_go=5)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-25.0, 25.0), window=(-8.5, 12.5))
plt.show()
```

**Count the threat. What kind of throw does the offense want, how fast, and where?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A hot throw, out in about a second and a half, and away from the cornerbacks' leverage.**
Count first. Nobody is deeper than about six yards: this is a "zero" look, with no deep safety at
all ([Cover 0](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd)). Zero lets the defense put a man on
every receiver and send everyone else. With five receivers out, that is six rushers against five
blockers. If the back stays in to block, his defender can come too: seven rushers against six
blockers. Either way one rusher is free, and nobody can hold the ball. That is the
[Cover 0 blitz](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd) bet: the defense is wagering
that the ball can't come out in time.

Now look at the cornerbacks. Both are pressed and both are a yard *inside* their receivers. That
is the leverage rule at work: with no safety anywhere, the corner has no help inside, so he
protects the middle and uses the sideline as his help. The slant, the quick game's favorite throw,
is the route he is sitting on. So the ball goes away from his leverage, outside. Two answers fit:

- **The outside receivers' fade or back-shoulder throw.** With no safety behind the corner, a
  receiver who wins outside off the line is one catch from a touchdown, and the quarterback can
  throw it as soon as the receiver clears the jam. It's not a high-percentage throw (a pressed
  corner is right on the receiver), which is why it isn't the answer every time.
- **The hot route into the space a blitzer leaves.** Some of the defenders crowding the line
  will cover and some will rush. The receiver whose nearest defender rushes is hot: he breaks
  into the space that defender just left, and the ball goes there at once.

Which side? The side the protection call says the free rusher is coming from, because that is
where the hot receiver is and where the quarterback has the least time. A now screen is a poor
choice: the cornerback is standing a yard away, so there is no cushion to run into.

For a real one, see the Super Bowl LVII touchdown to Skyy Moore in the Chiefs film room above:
seven rushers, Cover 0, ball out in 1.7 seconds to the flat.

The defense might be bluffing, of course: show zero, bring four, drop two into the throwing
lanes. That is exactly why the throw is a *read* of where the extra defenders went, not just a
reflex ([Zone Blitz and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: count them"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-count
#| fig-cap: "First-and-10. The offense lines up in trips to its right."
dfn = [D("WDE", "DE", 1.0, -4.6, "E"), D("WDT", "DT", 1.0, -0.8, "T"), D("SDT", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "T"),
       D("SDE", "DE", 1.0, 5.0, "E"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.6, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.5, 1.0, "M"),
       D("SS", "SS", 5.0, 4.4, "SS"), D("NB", "NB", 7.0, 12.4, "$"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.5, 19.8, "CB"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -16.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 14.0, -1.0, "FS")]
p = Play(trips_right(), dfn, los=30, to_go=10)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-25.0, 25.0), window=(-8.5, 17.5))
plt.show()
```

**The defense has loaded the box to stop the run. What quick throw does that invite, and why?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A quick screen to the trips side: a bubble to H, or a now screen to Z.** Start by counting.
The box (roughly the area between the offensive tackles, out to about five yards deep) holds
seven defenders: four linemen, two linebackers and a safety. Outside it on the right there are
only the cornerback and the $. Then run the three questions:

- **Numbers:** on the right, outside the box, the offense has three players (Y, H and Z) and the
  defense two. The safety who would usually be the third defender out there is standing beside the
  linebackers, in the box. That's the trade the defense made: an extra run defender inside, one
  fewer pass defender outside.
- **Leverage:** the cornerback and the $ are both off and roughly over their receivers, so
  the blockers start in the right place: Z can turn the cornerback out toward the sideline, and
  Y, starting inside the $, can block him from the inside while H runs between them.
- **Grass:** both are about seven yards off, and the nearest help, the deep safety, is
  fourteen yards away in the middle of the field. A bubble caught at the snap is five yards
  gained before anyone can touch it.

A run into the middle would face seven defenders with five linemen to block them (six if a
receiver comes in to help): the defense has the numbers inside. The
quick screen is how the offense "runs" outside the box instead, and it's why so many offenses
attach a bubble to their running plays ([Run-Pass Options](04-06-rpos.qmd)).
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- The **quick game** is the passing game's fast lane: a short drop, short routes and a rhythm
  throw, out in about **2.5 seconds or less**. It is roughly half of what NFL offenses throw.
- It exists for **three jobs**: beat the rush with the clock, keep the offense **on schedule**
  with high-percentage throws, and **stretch the run game sideways** by getting the ball to fast
  players in space. It trades depth for certainty and needs yards after the catch and a deep
  threat to keep the bargain.
- Most quick concepts put **two receivers on opposite sides of one defender**, high and low
  (slant-flat, hitch-seam, double slants) or inside and outside (stick), or both (snag's
  triangle), and the quarterback throws to the one that defender doesn't take. Spacing stretches
  the whole underneath coverage; the speed out beats one cornerback's alignment.
- Most of the decision is made **before the snap**: read the defender's **leverage**, cushion
  and help, and throw away from leverage.
- **Press** is the defense's answer to the quick game's timing; the receiver's answer is the
  **release, stem, stack and break**, and the **double move** punishes a defender who jumps the
  short route.
- **Now and bubble screens** punish soft and outnumbered alignments (numbers, leverage, grass).
  Against **the blitz**, the free rusher is the quarterback's, and the ball that comes out fast,
  into the space the blitzer left, is worth the most.

**Builds on:** [Passing Fundamentals](04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd) (the routes, drops and
stretches every concept here is made of) and [Pass Protection](04-02-pass-protection.qmd)
(hot routes, sight adjustments and the five-, six- and seven-man protections the quick game
leans on), with the defensive basics of
[A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd).

**Sets up:** [Dropback Concepts](04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) takes the same stretches deeper,
with more time and longer progressions; [Run-Pass Options](04-06-rpos.qmd) attaches the quick
throws and screens to runs; [Quarterback Play](04-07-quarterback-play.qmd) covers anticipation,
footwork and the numbers for judging accuracy. On the defensive side,
[Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) teaches press and off
coverage from the cornerback's side, and [Blitz and Man Pressure](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd)
does the blitz math from the defense's. [Concepts Versus Coverages](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd)
finally pairs each concept with the coverages it beats, and [Third Down](../10-situational-football/10-02-third-down.qmd)
shows where the quick game earns its keep.

**Case studies:** [Walsh's 49ers and the West Coast offense](../12-case-studies/12-01-walsh-49ers-west-coast.qmd)
and [Andy Reid's Chiefs](../12-case-studies/12-04-reid-chiefs.qmd).

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
- Bill Walsh, with Brian Billick and James A. Peterson, *Finding the Winning Edge* (1997): the
  coach's own account of how he built a passing game around timing and short throws.
- Chris B. Brown, *The Art of Smart Football* (2015) and *The Essential Smart Football* (2012),
  and his Smart Football site: clear essays on stick, snag, spacing and why they work.
- Tim Layden, *Blood, Sweat and Chalk* (2010): the chapter on Walsh traces the West Coast
  offense back to the Cincinnati years.
- **From diagrams to real tracking data.** The two animations above are gridiron simulations in
  NFL Big Data Bowl coordinates. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release (2022 season, weeks 1–9) records
  every player ten times a second, and its play and player files include each play's time to
  throw and each receiver's charted route, so you can find real quick throws and watch them. The
  data needs a free Kaggle login, so this code is not run when the book is built.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
player_play = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/player_play.csv")
# completed passes out in under 2.5 seconds on which some receiver ran a slant
quick = plays[(plays["timeToThrow"] < 2.5) & (plays["passResult"] == "C")]
slants = player_play.loc[player_play["routeRan"] == "SLANT", ["gameId", "playId"]].drop_duplicates()
cand = quick.merge(slants, on=["gameId", "playId"])
g, pl = cand.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.6])   # snap, release, break, catch
```
:::

[^ttt25]: Course calculation from nflverse participation data (`time_to_throw`, FTN-sourced), 2025 regular season: 17,394 pass attempts with a recorded time (sacks, spikes and scrambles excluded). Median 2.5 seconds; 48% of attempts left the quarterback's hand in under 2.5 seconds and 52% in 2.5 seconds or less. The 2.5-second line is an analysts' convention, not a rule; PFF, for one, splits time to throw there (PFF, "Signature Stat Snapshot: Time To Throw": https://www.pff.com/news/signature-stat-snapshot-time-to-throw).

[^ttt25b]: Course calculation, same data: attempts out in under 2.5 seconds were completed 72.2% of the time (success rate 51.5%), slower attempts 57.1% (success rate 44.9%). Success means positive EPA, the definition in [Expected Points, EPA and Success Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd).

[^yac]: Course calculation, same data: on 2025 completions thrown in under 2.5 seconds, 58.7% of receiving yards came after the catch; on slower completions, 38.5%. Screens are included, which pushes the quick figure up: about 23% of throws out in under 2 seconds were screens (FTN `is_screen_pass`).

[^walshrun]: Walsh to Tom FitzGerald of the *San Francisco Chronicle*: "We couldn't control the football with the run; [opposing] teams were just too strong. So it had to be the forward pass, and obviously it had to be a high-percentage, short, controlled passing game." The same profile describes his offense as "passes so short they were effectively extended handoffs." Both in "Walsh, Bill," *Encyclopedia.com*: https://www.encyclopedia.com/people/sports-and-games/sports-biographies/bill-walsh

[^carter]: Bill Walsh with Brian Billick and James A. Peterson, *Finding the Winning Edge* (Sports Publishing, 1997), on building the Bengals' short passing game around Virgil Carter. "West Coast offense," *Wikipedia*: Walsh "was tasked with devising an offensive plan suited to Bengal quarterback Virgil Carter, who had an accurate but relatively weak arm," and Carter "led the league in passing percentage in 1971": https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_offense . Carter completed 138 of 222 (62.2%), the NFL's best that season: Pro Football Reference, 1971 NFL leaders, https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1971/leaders.htm . Greg Cook tore the rotator cuff in his throwing shoulder in the third game of 1969, played through the season, then needed surgeries that kept him out of the next three seasons: "Greg Cook," *Wikipedia*, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Cook . The Bengals began play in 1968.

[^machol]: Virgil Carter and Robert E. Machol, "Operations Research on Football," *Operations Research* 19, no. 2 (1971): 541–544, which estimated the expected-point value of first-and-10 at each part of the field from 8,373 plays in the first 56 games of the 1969 NFL season: https://ideas.repec.org/a/inm/oropre/v19y1971i2p541-544.html . On Carter's statistics major at BYU and his MBA at Northwestern, taken while he played for the Bears: ESPN, "Ex-Bengals QB Virgil Carter's legacy of EPA, other analytics" (2024): https://www.espn.com.au/nfl/story/_/id/40276150/nfl-epa-analytics-virgil-carter-cincinnati-bengals

[^walsh]: Pro Football Hall of Fame, "Bill Walsh" (Class of 1993): head coach of the 49ers 1979–1988, winners of Super Bowls XVI, XIX and XXIII: https://www.profootballhof.com/players/bill-walsh/

[^rice]: Pro Football Hall of Fame, "Jerry Rice" (Class of 2010), including his 22 touchdown catches in the strike-shortened 12-game 1987 season, then an NFL record (Randy Moss caught 23 in 2007): https://www.profootballhof.com/players/jerry-rice/

[^blount]: Pro Football Hall of Fame, NFL history, 1978: "Rules changes permitted a defender to maintain contact with a receiver within five yards of the line of scrimmage, but restricted contact beyond that point": https://www.profootballhof.com/football-history/football-history/1960-1979/1978 ; and 1977: "Defenders were permitted to make contact with eligible receivers only once": https://www.profootballhof.com/football-history/football-history/1960-1979/1977 . The 1978 change is often called the "Mel Blount rule" (Steelers Depot, "Mel Blount explains play that created Mel Blount rule," 2024: https://steelersdepot.com/2024/02/mel-blount-explains-play-that-created-mel-blount-rule). The era is the subject of [The 1978 Liberation](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd).

[^chuck]: NFL Rulebook, Rule 8, Section 4 ("Legal and Illegal Contact With Eligible Receivers"), Articles 1–3: within the area five yards beyond the line of scrimmage, a defender may chuck an eligible receiver in front of him; beyond five yards, while the passer is still in the pocket with the ball, he may not initiate contact with a receiver who is trying to evade him (illegal contact: five yards and an automatic first down). Grabbing or restricting a receiver is defensive holding (Rule 12, Section 1): https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ ; NFL Video Rulebook, "Illegal Contact": https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-video-rulebook/illegal-contact . After the Patriots' physical coverage in the 2003 season's AFC Championship Game, the Competition Committee made illegal contact and defensive holding a point of emphasis for 2004: NBC Sports Boston, "They called it the 'Ty Law Rule'": https://www.nbcsportsboston.com/nfl/new-england-patriots/they-called-it-the-ty-law-rule-and-that-was-ok-with-him/393549/

[^opi]: NFL Video Rulebook, "Offensive Pass Interference": it is offensive pass interference for an offensive player to block more than one yard beyond the line of scrimmage before the pass is thrown, or to initiate contact with a defender in a way that restricts him while the pass is in the air: https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-video-rulebook/offensive-pass-interference . The rule is NFL Rule 8, Section 5 (Pass Interference); see https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ .

[^contested]: Course calculation from FTN charting (`is_contested_ball`) joined to nflverse play-by-play, 2025 regular season: 16,733 pass attempts excluding throwaways and spikes; 13.9% charted as contested. Completion rate 41.9% on contested throws, 71.1% on the rest. Contested throws went farther (12.7 yards in the air on average, against 7.1), which accounts for part of the gap.

[^backward]: NFL Rulebook, Rule 8, Section 7 ("Backward Pass and Fumble"): players of either team may catch a backward pass, or recover one after it touches the ground, and advance it; the special fourth-down and final-two-minutes limits on advancing apply to fumbles, not backward passes: https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/ ; NFL Video Rulebook, "Backward Pass": https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-video-rulebook/backward-pass

[^airraid]: Ralph D. Russo, "Air Raid evolution: Pioneering offense passes test of time," Associated Press, Aug. 24, 2022, on the offense "birthed from the mind of Hal Mumme" and "inspired by LaVell Edwards' BYU passing game and Bill Walsh's West Coast offense," whose "foundational concepts and plays" it lists as "mesh, Y cross, four verts, the quick game": https://kvia.com/ap-texas/2022/08/24/air-raid-evolution-pioneering-offense-passes-test-of-time/

[^rushepa]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play and participation data (`number_of_pass_rushers`, `time_to_throw`), 2025 regular season dropbacks with a charted rush count. "Quick" = a pass attempt out in under 2.5 seconds; "held" = an attempt out in 2.5 seconds or more, a sack, or a scramble. EPA per dropback: four or fewer rushers, quick +0.118 (n = 5,767) and held −0.014 (n = 8,708); five or more rushers, quick +0.226 (n = 2,532) and held −0.098 (n = 2,763). Five or more rushed on 27% of these dropbacks. Pooled over all outcomes, EPA per dropback was +0.054 against five or more rushers (n = 5,306; sack rate 7.8%) and +0.038 against four or fewer (n = 14,524; sack rate 6.0%); success rates 45.9% and 45.5%. Five or more rushed on 25% of first-down, 25% of second-down, 30% of third-down and 34% of fourth-down dropbacks, so the pooled comparison is not controlled for down and distance.

[^brees]: Pro Football Reference, Drew Brees career passing (2017: 386 of 536, 72.0%; 2018: 364 of 489, 74.4%), and the NFL record book (single-season completion percentage): https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/B/BreeDr00.htm . Guinness World Records lists 74.4% as the record (and 72.0% in 2017 as the mark it broke): https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/93395-highest-completion-percentage-nfl-season . In nflverse play-by-play no qualified passer from 2019 through 2025 topped 74.4% (the closest was Brees himself, about 74% in 2019). Payton was the Saints' head coach from 2006 to 2021 but was suspended for the 2012 season.

[^thomas]: NFL.com, "Saints' Michael Thomas sets NFL reception record" (Dec. 22, 2019), his 144th catch passing Marvin Harrison's 143 (2002): https://www.nfl.com/news/saints-michael-thomas-sets-nfl-reception-record-0ap3000001090697 ; he finished with 149 (NFL.com, "Saints WR Michael Thomas named 2019 NFL OPOY": https://www.nfl.com/news/saints-wr-michael-thomas-named-2019-nfl-opoy-0ap3000001100165). Course calculations from nflverse play-by-play and participation (NGS-sourced) data: 104 of Thomas's 149 catches (70%) came on throws of less than 10 air yards, and half within 5; Brees's 2019 time to throw averaged 2.57 s, second-fastest of 26 passers with 300+ attempts, with an average depth of target of about 6.5 yards.

[^welker]: Pro Football Reference, Wes Welker career receiving: 112 receptions (2007, tied for the NFL lead), 123 (2009, NFL lead), 122 (2011, NFL lead): https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WelkWe00.htm . The 2007 lead was shared with Cincinnati's T. J. Houshmandzadeh (also 112). In nflverse play-by-play, his targets in 2009–2012 averaged about 5.5 to 7.7 yards in the air, against a league average of about 8.2 to 8.7, and in 2007, 2009 and 2011 between 51% and 65% of his catches came on throws of 5 air yards or less.

[^brady]: Course calculation from nflverse participation data (`time_to_throw`, NGS-sourced), 2022 regular season, passers with 300 or more attempts: Brady averaged 2.45 seconds, fastest of 29. He was second-fastest in 2021.

[^kc2high]: Course calculation from nflverse participation data (`defense_coverage_type`, NGS-charted), regular-season dropbacks with a coverage label: Kansas City faced a two-high coverage (Cover 2, Cover 4, Cover 6 or 2-Man) on 45.8% of dropbacks in 2021 (3rd of 32), against a league average of 38.2%; in 2018 the figures were 35.6% and 32.9%. Kansas City's average depth of target fell from 9.06 yards in 2018 (5th deepest) to 8.55 in 2019 (13th), 8.11 in 2020 (15th) and 7.36 in 2021 (27th).

[^sb57]: nflverse play-by-play and participation (NGS charting), 2022 postseason, game `2022_22_KC_PHI`: 4th quarter, 9:26, third-and-goal at the Philadelphia 4, "P.Mahomes pass short left to S.Moore for 4 yards, TOUCHDOWN," time to throw 1.735 s, coverage charted COVER_0 (man), seven pass rushers; the Toney touchdown came at 12:08 (5 yards, time to throw 1.267 s). On the two plays as the same motion concept ("Corn Dog") run to opposite sides: CBS Sports, "'Corn dog' joins Chiefs Super Bowl lore: Andy Reid says Kadarius Toney TD came on a play with an unusual name": https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/corn-dog-joins-chiefs-super-bowl-lore-andy-reid-says-kadarius-toney-td-came-on-a-play-with-an-unusual-name ; Yahoo Sports, "The Xs and Os: How the Chiefs won the Super Bowl with a couple of 'Corn Dogs'": https://sports.yahoo.com/xs-os-chiefs-won-super-110132971.html

[^hill]: NFL.com, "Chiefs trading WR Tyreek Hill to Dolphins for multiple draft picks, including 2022 first-rounder" (March 23, 2022): five picks, the 2022 first-, second- and fourth-rounders and 2023 fourth- and sixth-rounders: https://www.nfl.com/news/chiefs-trading-wr-tyreek-hill-to-dolphins-for-multiple-draft-picks

[^kc]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular season: Kansas City's average depth of target was 9.06 yards in 2018 (5th deepest of 32), 7.24 in 2022 (23rd), 6.47 in 2023 and 6.37 in 2024 (31st both years), and 7.80 in 2025 (17th). Travis Kelce drew 153 targets in 2022, 72.5% of them under 10 air yards.
